frames.narration: A user uploads a photo. It gets a 64-bit id, and four sizes are made. The photo store appends one needle for each size to the end of the open store file. Each needle has a header, the image data and a footer, and the four share the photo's key and differ in the alternate key that holds the size.

The photo store notes where each new needle starts. It adds four entries to its in-memory index, one per size, each a photo id and size mapped to an offset in the store file. Each entry costs about 2 bits of overhead in the sparse hash structure the post names.
Later a browser asks for the medium size of that photo. The CDN does not have it, because the photo is rarely viewed, so the request goes to the photo store.

The photo store looks the photo and size up in memory and gets an offset. No disk is touched yet. Compare the old design, where finding the file meant reading directory and inode metadata that was not in any cache.
One disk read at that offset returns the needle, and it fetches only photo data. The photo store sends it back through the CDN, which may keep it for next time.

The user deletes the photo. The photo store only sets a flag on its needles and removes them from the index. The bytes stay in the file, because the file is append-only. Reads for the photo now find nothing in the index.

Compaction runs online. It copies the live needles into a new store file and leaves the flagged ones behind, so the space comes back, and the new file replaces the old one while the machine keeps serving.

messages.label: copy live needles to a new file
